learning_path.title: Understand the AuthBase callable contract via HTTPBasicAuth.__call__
learning_path.why: This is the core contract: every auth handler is a callable that receives a PreparedRequest, mutates its headers, and returns it — understanding this pattern unlocks how all auth integrates into the request pipeline.
learning_path.understand: Auth handlers are not middleware or decorators; they are plain callables invoked with a fully-assembled PreparedRequest, and they signal their result by returning the same object after mutation.

learning_path.title: See how HTTPProxyAuth specialises the same callable contract for proxy headers
learning_path.why: Comparing HTTPProxyAuth to HTTPBasicAuth shows that the callable contract is general enough to target any header, and the only difference between request auth and proxy auth is which header key is written.
learning_path.understand: Subclassing HTTPBasicAuth and overriding __call__ to write a different header is the entire extension surface for new credential-injection strategies.

learning_path.title: Trace how auth is wired into Request at construction time
learning_path.why: The Request class is where the user supplies an auth handler or (user, pass) tuple; understanding what gets stored here explains what flows into preparation.
learning_path.understand: Request stores auth as an opaque value — it can be a callable object, a two-tuple, or None — deferring the actual header mutation until prepare() is called.

learning_path.title: Understand why prepare_auth must be called last inside PreparedRequest.prepare
learning_path.why: The explicit comment in prepare() that 'prepare_auth must be last' reveals a critical ordering invariant: auth handlers receive a fully-formed request so they can sign over the complete content (e.g. OAuth body hashing).
learning_path.understand: The pipeline order — method → url → headers → cookies → body → auth → hooks — is a deliberate API contract; auth runs after body preparation precisely so schemes like OAuth can sign the full payload.

learning_path.title: Follow Session.__init__ to see how session-level auth is stored as a default
learning_path.why: Session.auth acts as a fallback when no per-request auth is provided; knowing it exists and that it is merged at send-time explains why authentication set on the session propagates to every request.
learning_path.understand: Session-level auth (self.auth = None by default) is a convenience default that gets merged with per-request auth, with the per-request value winning when both are supplied.

learning_path.title: Understand how auth credentials are stripped and reapplied safely during redirects
learning_path.why: rebuild_auth is where credential leakage is prevented: it deletes the Authorization header when redirecting to a different host and then gives .netrc a chance to supply new credentials for the new host.
learning_path.understand: The should_strip_auth check on every redirect is the security boundary that prevents credentials from being forwarded to an unintended origin, and trust_env controls whether .netrc can re-authenticate after stripping.

learning_path.title: Trace auth from top-level request() into Session
learning_path.why: This is the true entry point for auth flow — Session.request() accepts the auth parameter, wraps it in a Request object, and hands off to prepare_request where merging and resolution happen.
learning_path.understand: Auth starts as a raw parameter here and gets passed into the preparation pipeline; Session.request() is where the user-facing auth value first enters the system.

learning_path.title: Understand how session-level and request-level auth are merged
learning_path.why: prepare_request() is where auth priority is resolved: netrc is consulted only when trust_env is set and no explicit auth exists, then merge_setting() picks request auth over session auth for non-dict values.
learning_path.understand: The precedence order is: explicit request auth > session.auth > netrc — and merge_setting is the non-obvious mechanism that implements this for non-dict values by simply returning the request setting.

learning_path.title: Understand merge_setting's precedence logic for auth callables
learning_path.why: Auth values are callables or tuples, not Mappings, so merge_setting short-circuits at the isinstance check and returns the request_setting directly — a non-obvious but critical detail.
learning_path.understand: For non-Mapping types like auth callables, merge_setting always returns the request-level value if present, making request auth unconditionally override session auth without any merging.

learning_path.title: See how PreparedRequest.prepare() sequences auth last
learning_path.why: prepare() explicitly positions prepare_auth after all other preparation steps and before prepare_hooks, enabling auth schemes like OAuth to sign a fully-formed request and register hooks.
learning_path.understand: Auth must run last among the prepare_* methods because auth handlers may need to sign the final URL, headers, and body — and may register response hooks — so ordering here is a correctness invariant.

learning_path.title: Examine how prepare_auth resolves URL-embedded credentials and 2-tuples
learning_path.why: prepare_auth contains two important implicit conversions: URL-embedded credentials are extracted as a fallback, and bare (username, password) 2-tuples are silently promoted to HTTPBasicAuth.
learning_path.understand: Auth normalization happens here — a tuple becomes HTTPBasicAuth, URL credentials are a last resort, and the auth handler is then called as a callable to mutate self in-place via __dict__.update.

learning_path.title: Understand the AuthBase contract and extension point
learning_path.why: AuthBase defines the single-method contract: __call__ receives a PreparedRequest and must return a PreparedRequest, making any callable with this signature a valid auth handler.
learning_path.understand: The entire auth system is duck-typed around __call__(PreparedRequest) -> PreparedRequest — AuthBase just documents this contract and raises NotImplementedError; you don't need to inherit from it at all.

learning_path.title: See HTTPBasicAuth's minimal __call__ implementation
learning_path.why: HTTPBasicAuth.__call__ shows the simplest possible auth implementation: mutate one header and return self — three lines that every custom auth handler can mirror.
learning_path.understand: Basic auth is entirely stateless and synchronous — no hooks, no retry logic — making it the clearest reference implementation for the AuthBase contract.

learning_path.title: Study HTTPDigestAuth.__call__'s stateful hook-based approach
learning_path.why: Digest auth can't authenticate upfront without a server nonce, so __call__ registers a response hook (handle_401) and relies on a thread-local to carry state across the initial and retry requests.
learning_path.understand: Unlike BasicAuth, DigestAuth uses the hook system and per-thread state to implement a challenge-response flow — the first request goes out unauthenticated or with a cached nonce, and the hook handles the 401 retry.

learning_path.title: Trace the 401 retry path inside HTTPDigestAuth.handle_401
learning_path.why: handle_401 is the response hook registered in __call__ — it parses the WWW-Authenticate header, rebuilds the PreparedRequest with a real digest header, and re-sends it on the same connection.
learning_path.understand: The retry bypasses Session.request entirely by calling r.connection.send(prep) directly, which means session-level hooks and settings are not re-applied — a sharp edge when debugging digest auth failures.

dossier.understanding: Authentication in requests is applied through a callable-based handler pattern. When preparing an outgoing request, the library treats auth as either a tuple (for basic auth) or a callable object conforming to AuthBase. The auth parameter flows through the request preparation pipeline: it's optionally extracted from the URL, merged with session-level auth settings (request auth takes precedence), and applied in PreparedRequest.prepare_auth by invoking the auth handler as a callable that modifies request headers and returns the modified request. This allows arbitrary authentication strategies through custom handlers while providing built-in support for HTTPBasicAuth and HTTPDigestAuth.

learning_path.title: See the simplest concrete implementation: HTTPBasicAuth.__call__
learning_path.why: HTTPBasicAuth is the canonical one-liner implementation of the protocol: mutate the Authorization header and return the request — it makes the contract concrete and shows the minimum viable auth handler.
learning_path.understand: A compliant auth handler only needs to set headers (or other request attributes) and return the same PreparedRequest object; no subclassing beyond AuthBase is strictly required.

learning_path.title: Study HTTPDigestAuth.__call__ and its deferred-auth pattern via hooks
learning_path.why: Digest auth cannot complete in a single __call__ because it needs the server's WWW-Authenticate challenge — it registers a response hook for handle_401, revealing a second extension pattern beyond simple header mutation.
learning_path.understand: When cached nonce state exists the Authorization header is set eagerly; otherwise __call__ only registers handle_401 as a response hook and sets up body-position bookkeeping for the retry.

learning_path.title: Follow handle_401: the challenge-response retry loop for Digest auth
learning_path.why: handle_401 is where Digest auth actually completes: it parses the WWW-Authenticate header, copies and re-signs the request, and re-sends it — understanding this reveals the risk of infinite loops and the num_401_calls guard.
learning_path.understand: The method closes the original response, deep-copies the PreparedRequest, builds the real digest header from the parsed challenge, and fires a second send — the num_401_calls < 2 guard is the only thing preventing an infinite retry loop on persistent 401s.

learning_path.title: See how URL-embedded credentials are extracted as a last-resort fallback
learning_path.why: get_auth_from_url is called inside prepare_auth when auth is None, making URL credentials a silent fallback that developers may not realise is active — understanding it closes the complete precedence picture.
learning_path.understand: If no auth is supplied at the request or session level, prepare_auth silently extracts and uses credentials embedded in the URL (e.g. https://user:pass@host/); this is the lowest-precedence source and can cause unexpected authentication if URLs are constructed programmatically.

steps.what_happens: Module-level function receives method='GET', url, and kwargs including auth=('user', 'pass'). Creates a Session and calls session.request(method, url, auth=auth).
Creates a Request object with auth=('user', 'pass'), then calls self.prepare_request(req).
Extracts auth from request.auth, merges with self.auth via merge_setting(auth, self.auth). Passes merged auth to p.prepare(auth=merged_auth).
Calls prepare_method, prepare_url, prepare_headers, prepare_cookies, prepare_body, then prepare_auth(auth, url) and prepare_hooks.
Receives auth=('user', 'pass'). Checks if it's a tuple of length 2 and converts to HTTPBasicAuth(*auth). Calls auth_handler(self) which is HTTPBasicAuth.__call__(self).
Receives the PreparedRequest r. Calls _basic_auth_str(self.username, self.password) to create 'Basic <base64>' string. Sets r.headers['Authorization'] = authstr. Returns r.
User calls requests.get(url, auth=HTTPDigestAuth('user', 'pass')). Creates ephemeral Session and calls session.request().

learning_path.why: dispatch_hook is called on the Response object after Session.send, allowing user-registered callbacks to inspect or mutate the response before it is returned to the caller.

learning_path.title: See how api.request() spins up a Session

learning_path.title: Understand Session.request(): where the Request object is assembled
learning_path.why: Session.request() is the orchestration hub — it constructs a Request, triggers preparation, merges environment settings, and calls send().

learning_path.title: See how Session.prepare_request() merges session state into the request
learning_path.why: This is where per-request values (headers, cookies, auth, params) are merged with session-level defaults before the PreparedRequest is built.

learning_path.title: Trace PreparedRequest.prepare(): encoding the request to wire format
learning_path.why: This is where the abstract Request becomes concrete bytes: method normalization, URL encoding, header validation, cookie serialization, body encoding, and auth application all happen here in a fixed order.

learning_path.why: get_adapter() reveals the extension point that lets you swap in custom transports (e.g. file://, mock adapters) by registering a prefix in session.adapters.

learning_path.title: Trace HTTPAdapter.send(): urllib3 call and exception translation
learning_path.why: This is where the actual TCP connection is made via urllib3's conn.urlopen(), and where every urllib3/socket exception is caught and re-raised as a requests-specific exception type.

learning_path.title: Understand Response.content: lazy body consumption and connection release
learning_path.why: This property is the final step in the flow — it reads and buffers all bytes from the raw urllib3 stream, and once consumed the connection is returned to the pool automatically by urllib3.
learning_path.understand: Accessing .content (or .text/.json which call it) is idempotent after the first read because the bytes are cached in _content, but calling it a second time after stream consumption raises RuntimeError — and the connection release is handled transparently by urllib3 on exhaustion.

learning_path.title: Trace how a Depends is converted into a child Dependant node
learning_path.why: get_parameterless_sub_dependant is the bridge between a params.Depends declaration and a fully-formed Dependant node in the dependency tree.

learning_path.title: Walk the full runtime resolution loop in solve_dependencies

learning_path.title: Understand the Depends annotation as the DI entry point
learning_path.why: Every dependency in FastAPI starts with a Depends instance; understanding its three fields (dependency callable, use_cache, scope) sets the vocabulary for everything downstream.
learning_path.understand: Depends is a frozen dataclass — a pure data carrier with no logic — whose three fields control what gets called, whether its result is reused per request, and whether teardown is scoped to a function call or the full request lifetime.

learning_path.title: Map the Dependant tree structure that represents resolved dependencies
learning_path.why: Dependant is the internal IR that get_dependant produces and solve_dependencies consumes; its fields directly encode every category of injectable value plus the recursive sub-dependency list.
learning_path.understand: A Dependant is a node in a dependency tree: it holds the callable to invoke, lists of typed parameter fields (path, query, body, etc.), a list of child Dependant nodes for sub-dependencies, and cached_property computations (cache_key, computed_scope, is_gen_callable) that drive resolution strategy at runtime.

learning_path.title: Trace how get_dependant builds the Dependant tree from a function signature
learning_path.why: This is the static analysis phase: it walks every parameter of the callable, dispatches to analyze_param, and either recurses into a sub-Dependant for Depends-annotated params or appends a ModelField to the appropriate param list.
learning_path.understand: get_dependant iterates signature parameters in one pass — when analyze_param returns a depends, it recursively calls get_dependant on the sub-dependency (propagating oauth scopes) and appends the result to dependant.dependencies; for everything else it appends a ModelField to the correct param bucket; scope violation (request-scoped dep depending on function-scoped dep) is asserted here at build time.

learning_path.title: Understand how analyze_param classifies each parameter into depends vs field
learning_path.why: This is where annotation introspection happens: it extracts Annotated metadata, resolves Depends from either the annotation or the default value, and falls back to heuristic field-type inference (Path/Query/Body/File) for plain typed params.

learning_path.title: See how route-level (parameterless) dependencies are injected at APIRoute init
learning_path.why: APIRoute.__init__ is where the static DI graph is assembled for an endpoint: it calls get_dependant for the endpoint callable, then prepends route-level Depends (via get_parameterless_sub_dependant) as head nodes in dependant.dependencies.
learning_path.understand: Route-level dependencies declared on the APIRouter or decorator are inserted at index 0 of dependant.dependencies in reverse order so they resolve before the endpoint's own dependencies — this is the architectural seam where per-router auth or rate-limit dependencies attach without touching endpoint signatures.

learning_path.title: Understand get_parameterless_sub_dependant as the bridge for router-level deps
learning_path.why: This thin function converts a bare Depends object (no param name) into a full Dependant node so it can be prepended to dependant.dependencies alongside signature-derived sub-dependants.
learning_path.understand: get_parameterless_sub_dependant calls get_dependant with only a path and the dependency callable (no name), making router-level dependencies structurally identical to inline Depends params so the solver can process them uniformly.

learning_path.title: Deep-dive the SolvedDependency result container
learning_path.why: SolvedDependency is the output contract of solve_dependencies; its fields (values, errors, background_tasks, response, dependency_cache) are exactly what the request handler reads to either call the endpoint or raise a validation error.
learning_path.understand: SolvedDependency carries the merged kwargs dict (values) ready to splat into the endpoint, the accumulated validation errors list, and the shared dependency_cache dict that is threaded through all recursive solve_dependencies calls to implement use_cache deduplication.

learning_path.title: Trace solve_dependencies: recursive resolution, caching, generator lifecycle, and scope handling
learning_path.why: This async function is the runtime core of DI: it recurses depth-first through the Dependant tree, applies dependency_overrides, uses dependency_cache to deduplicate, routes generators to the correct AsyncExitStack (request vs function scope), and aggregates kwargs and errors.
learning_path.understand: solve_dependencies implements post-order DFS — sub-dependencies are fully solved before the parent is called; the cache_key (callable + oauth scopes + computed_scope) is checked before calling, and generator dependencies are entered into either the request-scoped or function-scoped AsyncExitStack based on sub_dependant.scope, meaning teardown order and lifetime are structurally enforced, not left to user code.

learning_path.title: See how get_request_handler wires the solved DI result into actual endpoint invocation
learning_path.why: get_request_handler is where the DI output (solved_result.values) is finally splatted into the endpoint callable, completing the full request-handling flow from HTTP body parsing through dependency resolution to response serialization.
learning_path.understand: The inner app coroutine calls solve_dependencies with the assembled dependant and passes solved_result.values directly to the endpoint; if solved_result.errors is non-empty the endpoint is never called and a RequestValidationError is raised instead — making the DI layer the authoritative validation gate before any application logic runs.

dossier.understanding: FastAPI's dependency injection system is a declarative framework for declaring function parameters as dependencies via the `Depends()` annotation, which FastAPI then automatically resolves and injects at request time. The system has three phases: (1) **Analysis** — at route definition time, FastAPI inspects the endpoint function's signature and builds a tree structure (`Dependant`) representing all dependencies and their parameters; (2) **Resolution** — at request time, FastAPI recursively solves each dependency by calling its callable with recursively-solved sub-dependencies and extracted request data (path/query/body params); (3) **Injection** — the resolved values are passed as kwargs to the endpoint and its dependency callables. Dependencies can be nested, cached per-request, and conditional on OAuth scopes, and they support cleanup via generator patterns (yield-based context managers).

contracts.contract: A Depends object holds `dependency: Callable[..., Any] | None`, `use_cache: bool`, and `scope: Literal['function', 'request'] | None`. It is created by the user as a default value or within Annotated to mark a parameter as a dependency. The callable can be a function, a class, or a callable object, and FastAPI will call it with its own dependencies recursively resolved.

A Dependant models a callable and its parameters. It holds `call: Callable | None`, `dependencies: list[Dependant]` (sub-dependencies), parameter lists (`path_params`, `query_params`, `body_params`, etc., each a list of ModelField), and metadata flags (`use_cache`, `scope`). Properties like `is_coroutine_callable`, `is_gen_callable`, `is_async_gen_callable` indicate how to invoke the callable.

Takes a Dependant tree and an incoming Request, and returns a SolvedDependency. It must recursively resolve all sub-dependencies, extract request data, handle caching based on use_cache and cache_key, detect and call async/sync/generator callables appropriately, and return a values dict suitable for **kwargs to the endpoint.

learning_path.understand: The Dependant tree is constructed eagerly during route registration — not per request — and route-level dependencies are inserted at index 0 in reverse order so they resolve before endpoint-level ones.

learning_path.title: Study the Dependant model and its cached properties
learning_path.why: Dependant is the central data structure every other piece operates on; its cached properties encode both the runtime dispatch logic and the caching identity used per request.
learning_path.understand: cache_key is a tuple of (callable, sorted oauth scopes, computed_scope) used to deduplicate resolved dependencies; computed_scope defaults to 'request' for generator callables and None otherwise, which governs which AsyncExitStack manages teardown.

learning_path.title: Follow get_dependant to see how a function signature becomes a Dependant tree
learning_path.why: get_dependant is the recursive compile-time analyzer that converts a Python function's type annotations into a Dependant with typed parameter lists and nested sub-Dependants.
learning_path.understand: For each parameter, get_dependant calls analyze_param() and either recurses into itself for Depends parameters (building the sub-tree) or classifies the parameter into path/query/header/cookie/body lists; a scope-mismatch guard raises DependencyScopeError if a request-scoped generator depends on a function-scoped dependency.

learning_path.title: Understand how analyze_param classifies a single parameter
learning_path.why: analyze_param is the innermost classification engine; it handles Annotated metadata, default-value Depends, bare FieldInfo, and the implicit inference rules (UploadFile→File, complex type→Body, scalar→Query).
learning_path.understand: Resolution priority is: Annotated FastAPI annotation wins over default value; if a Depends has no explicit dependency callable, the type annotation itself is used as the callable; field type inference only fires when neither depends nor field_info was found.

learning_path.title: See how special injected types bypass field resolution
learning_path.why: add_non_field_param_to_dependency handles the injection of raw Starlette/FastAPI objects that are never parsed from the request body — they are stored by name on the Dependant and injected directly in solve_dependencies.
learning_path.understand: These six types (Request, WebSocket, HTTPConnection, Response, BackgroundTasks, SecurityScopes) are detected by subclass check and stored as named slots on the Dependant, completely bypassing Pydantic field validation.

learning_path.title: Deep-dive solve_dependencies — the per-request resolver
learning_path.why: solve_dependencies is the runtime heart of dependency injection: it recursively resolves sub-Dependants, enforces caching via dependency_cache, dispatches to the right async stack for generator teardown, and assembles the final values dict.
learning_path.understand: Sub-dependencies are resolved depth-first via recursion; generator dependencies are entered on either the request-scoped or function-scoped AsyncExitStack depending on computed_scope; caching uses cache_key so the same callable with the same scopes is only invoked once per request regardless of how many places declare it.

learning_path.title: See how solved values wire into the endpoint call in get_request_handler
learning_path.why: get_request_handler is the per-request closure that calls solve_dependencies, checks validation errors, and calls the endpoint with solved_result.values — closing the loop between compile-time analysis and runtime execution.
learning_path.understand: dependency_overrides_provider is threaded through here into solve_dependencies, making dependency overrides a runtime substitution at the call-graph level rather than at the Dependant tree level, which is why overrides work in tests without re-registering routes.

dossier.understanding: FastAPI's dependency injection system works in two main phases: **compile-time analysis** and **runtime resolution**. At compile time, when an APIRoute is created, `get_dependant()` introspects the endpoint function's signature using `analyze_param()` to identify dependencies (marked with `Depends()` or `Security()`), regular parameters (query, path, header, cookie, body), and special injected types (Request, Response, BackgroundTasks, etc.). This builds a tree of `Dependant` objects representing nested dependencies. At runtime, when a request arrives, `solve_dependencies()` recursively resolves the dependency tree by calling each dependency function with its own resolved arguments, caching results, extracting values from request (path params, query, headers, cookies, body), and injecting special types. The resolved values are then passed to the endpoint function via `**solved_result.values`. This design separates parameter analysis (which is expensive and happens once per route) from value resolution (which happens per request) and enables scoping, caching, security, and automatic validation.

components.role_in_goal: Core data structure that represents a dependency or endpoint function with all its parameters, sub-dependencies, and special injected types. Stores the callable, parameter lists (path/query/header/cookie/body), child dependencies, caching config, and scope information.
components.why_it_matters: To understand DI, you must know what information is extracted and stored about each function. Dependant is the tree node that holds this metadata.

components.role_in_goal: Analyzes a function signature and constructs a Dependant tree by calling analyze_param() on each parameter, identifying Depends() markers, building sub-Dependants recursively, and classifying other parameters into path/query/header/cookie/body fields. This is the main compile-time analysis function.
components.why_it_matters: This function is where the DI system learns what a function needs. It's called once per route to build the dependency graph that will be used for every request.

components.role_in_goal: Examines a single function parameter to determine if it's a dependency (Depends/Security), a request parameter (Query/Path/Header/Cookie/Body/Form/File), or a special injected type. Returns ParamDetails with the findings. Handles Annotated syntax and default value unpacking.
components.why_it_matters: This is where individual parameters are classified. Understanding it shows how FastAPI distinguishes between dependencies, request parameters, and injected types.

components.role_in_goal: The runtime resolution engine. Recursively resolves sub-dependencies, extracts values from request (path/query/header/cookie/body), injects special types (Request, Response, BackgroundTasks, SecurityScopes), handles caching per dependency scope, manages async context cleanup via AsyncExitStack, and returns all resolved values as a dict keyed by parameter name.
components.why_it_matters: This function executes every request. It implements the runtime contract that turns a Dependant tree and a request into resolved function arguments. Must understand: caching logic, async/sync execution paths, scoping, and value injection.

components.role_in_goal: Detects special injected types (Request, WebSocket, HTTPConnection, Response, BackgroundTasks, SecurityScopes) and records their parameter names in the Dependant for injection during solve_dependencies.
components.why_it_matters: Shows how FastAPI provides implicit access to request/response objects without explicit Depends(). These types are injected automatically by name matching.

components.role_in_goal: Frozen dataclass marking a parameter as a dependency. Holds the dependency callable, use_cache flag (for request-scoped caching), and scope (function or request). Used as a marker in function signatures and Annotated.
components.why_it_matters: The syntactic token users write to declare a dependency. Understanding its structure (frozen dataclass with callable, cache, scope) is essential to understand how dependencies are identified and configured.

components.role_in_goal: Subclass of Depends that adds OAuth2 scopes. Used to declare dependencies that are security schemes and require specific scopes.
components.why_it_matters: Shows how the DI system is extended to support security. Security scopes are propagated through the dependency tree and passed to security scheme functions.

components.role_in_goal: Creates an APIRoute and calls get_dependant() to analyze the endpoint function. Also processes route-level dependencies (dependencies parameter) by inserting them into the dependant tree. Stores the dependant for later use by get_route_handler.
components.why_it_matters: Entry point where DI analysis is triggered. Shows when and how the dependency tree is built, and how route-level dependencies are merged with endpoint-level dependencies.

components.role_in_goal: Generates the async request handler that receives a request and returns a response. This handler calls solve_dependencies to resolve all parameters, then calls the endpoint function with the resolved values, and serializes the result. This is where compile-time analysis (Dependant) meets runtime execution.
components.why_it_matters: The bridge between the static dependency tree and the dynamic request/response cycle. Shows how resolved dependencies become function arguments and how errors are caught.

entry_points.how_it_enters: When a route is defined via @app.get(), @app.post(), etc., an APIRoute is instantiated. In __init__ (lines 949-950), get_dependant() is called to analyze the endpoint function and build the dependency tree. This is the entry point to compile-time DI analysis.

When a request arrives matching the route, the handler returned by get_request_handler (a closure named 'app') is called with the request. Inside, solve_dependencies is called (line 457) to resolve all dependencies and extract all parameter values at runtime.

flows.name: Compile-time dependency analysis (when APIRoute is created)

steps.what_happens: APIRoute.__init__ calls get_dependant(path=path, call=endpoint, scope='function') at line 949 to analyze the endpoint function.
get_dependant extracts the endpoint's signature via get_typed_signature(), then iterates over each parameter (line 309) and calls analyze_param for each one.

For each parameter, analyze_param (lines 393-559) checks if it's wrapped in Annotated, extracts FastAPI annotations (Depends, Security, Query, Path, etc.), infers the type, and determines the parameter kind. Returns ParamDetails with the annotation, depends marker, or field info.

Back in get_dependant, if param_details.depends is not None (line 317), a recursive call to get_dependant (line 334) is made for the dependency function, building a Dependant tree. If not a depends, add_non_field_param_to_dependency is called (line 345) to detect special types, or the parameter is added to path_params/query_params/etc.

The returned Dependant tree is stored as self.dependant. Route-level dependencies (self.dependencies, line 925) are then inserted into the tree as additional sub-dependants (lines 952-956). A flattened version is created and stored for body field extraction.

flows.name: Runtime dependency resolution (when a request arrives)

steps.what_happens: The request handler function 'app' (defined line 382) receives the request. Body is parsed if present (lines 402-449). Then solve_dependencies is called (line 457) with the dependant tree, request, and body.

solve_dependencies recursively processes each sub-dependant (line 628). For each sub-dependant, it checks for dependency overrides (lines 632-647), then recursively calls itself to resolve that dependency's parameters (line 649).

After sub-dependencies are resolved, the sub-dependant's callable is invoked (lines 666-680): if it's a generator/async-gen, _solve_generator wraps it in an async context; if async, it's awaited; if sync, it's run in a thread pool. The result is cached if use_cache is True (lines 664-684).

Request parameters (path, query, header, cookie, body) are extracted and validated via request_params_to_args and request_body_to_args (lines 685-712). Special types are injected: Request, WebSocket, Response, BackgroundTasks, SecurityScopes (lines 713-728).

All resolved values (from sub-dependencies, request parameters, and injected types) are merged into a single dict keyed by parameter name (lines 697-712). A SolvedDependency is returned with the values dict and any errors (line 729).
The endpoint function is called with **solved_result.values (e.g., line 498 for SSE, line 622 for JSONL, line 674 for normal endpoints). The return value is serialized to a response.

get_dependant calls analyze_param for each parameter to classify it as a dependency, request parameter, or special type.
get_dependant recursively calls itself for each Depends/Security parameter to build the dependency tree.
analyze_param doesn't directly call this; get_dependant does. It detects special injected types like Request and Response.
Called to detect and record special types (Request, Response, etc.) that should be auto-injected.
The request handler calls solve_dependencies at runtime to resolve all dependencies and extract parameter values.
Recursively resolves sub-dependencies by calling itself on each sub-dependant.

contracts.contract: A Dependant represents a callable (function, dependency, or endpoint) with metadata about its parameters. It exposes: call (the callable), path_params/query_params/header_params/cookie_params/body_params (ModelField lists for request parameters), dependencies (list of sub-Dependants), and parameter names for special injected types (request_param_name, response_param_name, etc.). Properties like is_coroutine_callable and cache_key are computed. Implementers must populate this structure; callers depend on these lists and properties being accurate.

Analyzes a callable's signature and returns a Dependant representing it. Takes: path (route path string), call (the callable), name, oauth_scopes, use_cache, scope. Must introspect the callable, classify each parameter, recurse on dependencies, and return a fully populated Dependant tree. Callers pass this result to solve_dependencies or store it on routes.

Resolves a dependency tree against a request, returning a SolvedDependency with a dict of parameter values keyed by name. Takes: request, dependant, body (parsed request body), background_tasks, response, dependency_overrides_provider, dependency_cache, async_exit_stack, embed_body_fields. Must recursively resolve sub-dependencies, extract request parameters, validate them, call dependency functions, cache results, and inject special types. Callers pass the result's values dict to the endpoint function as **kwargs.

Analyzes a single function parameter and returns ParamDetails with: type_annotation (the inferred type), depends (Depends/Security marker if found), field (ModelField for request parameters). Must unpack Annotated, detect FastAPI markers, infer types, and classify the parameter. Called by get_dependant for each parameter.

A frozen dataclass marking a parameter as a dependency. Has: dependency (the callable to invoke), use_cache (bool, default True), scope (function or request, default None). Implementers create instances via Depends(callable) or Depends(callable, scope='request'). Analyzers check isinstance(value, Depends) to detect dependencies and read these fields.

prerequisites.why_needed: Dependant is a dataclass, Depends and Security are frozen dataclasses. Must understand field definitions, immutability, and how to instantiate them.
get_dependant uses inspect.signature to extract function parameters, and analyze_param uses inspect to check if annotations are empty. Must understand how to introspect callables.
analyze_param uses get_origin and get_args to unpack Annotated[type, FastAPI(...)] syntax. Must understand how Annotated works and how to extract metadata from it.
solve_dependencies checks is_coroutine_callable, is_gen_callable, is_async_gen_callable, and handles async execution and cleanup via AsyncExitStack. Must understand async execution models.
Parameters are converted to ModelField instances which use Pydantic for validation. Must understand how Pydantic validates and serializes values.
Resolved dependencies become a dict of values which is unpacked as **kwargs when calling the endpoint function. Must understand how dict unpacking works with function calls.

evidence_refs.clarifies: Lines 949-950 show that get_dependant is called during APIRoute.__init__, proving DI analysis happens at route creation time, not per-request. Lines 952-956 show how route-level dependencies are merged into the tree.

Lines 457-464 show solve_dependencies is called in the request handler with the Dependant tree, proving DI resolution happens per-request. Line 498 (and similar lines 622, 674) show the endpoint function is called with **solved_result.values, proving resolved dependencies become function arguments.

Lines 309-316 show analyze_param is called for each parameter, with the results used to classify parameters. Lines 317-344 show Depends is detected and recursively resolved. Lines 345-358 show other parameters are classified.

Lines 628-684 show sub-dependencies are recursively resolved (line 649), dependency functions are invoked (lines 678-680), and results are cached (lines 664-684). Lines 685-728 show request parameters are extracted and special types are injected. Line 729 returns all values.

Lines 393-559 show analyze_param's logic: lines 411-457 unpack Annotated and extract FastAPI annotations, lines 488-517 infer parameter kinds, lines 520-547 create ModelField for validation. Line 559 returns ParamDetails.

context: Dependency caching is controlled by the use_cache flag (default True). When use_cache=True, the dependency result is cached in dependency_cache keyed by cache_key (line 664-684 in solve_dependencies). This allows the same dependency to be called once per request even if multiple parameters depend on it.

Scopes control when a dependency is cached: 'request' scope (default) caches across the request; 'function' scope (only for generators) caches only within that generator's lifetime. The scope is stored in Dependant and checked in solve_dependencies to determine which AsyncExitStack to use for cleanup.

Security scopes are accumulated through the dependency tree. Each Security(dependency, scopes=[...]) adds its scopes to parent_oauth_scopes of sub-dependants (lines 331-339 in get_dependant). The SecurityScopes object passed to security functions contains the full accumulated scopes.

Dependency overrides are supported: solve_dependencies checks dependency_overrides_provider to allow test code to substitute a different callable for a dependency (lines 632-647). This is used in testing to mock dependencies.

Special injected types (Request, Response, BackgroundTasks, SecurityScopes) are auto-injected without explicit Depends(). They are detected by add_non_field_param_to_dependency and their parameter names are recorded in Dependant, then values are injected in solve_dependencies (lines 713-728).

Parameters can be specified in multiple ways: as Depends(callable) in default value, as Depends(callable) in Annotated, as Query(...), Path(...), etc. in default or Annotated, or inferred from type (defaults to Query for scalars, Body for complex types, Path for route params).

learning_path.title: Understand SecurityBase as the root extension point
learning_path.why: The DI system resolves security dependencies by asserting the callable is a SecurityBase instance — any custom scheme must subclass SecurityBase to be recognized.
learning_path.understand: FastAPI's dependency resolver detects security schemes by unwrapping the dependency callable and asserting isinstance(unwrapped, SecurityBase); your custom class must inherit from SecurityBase to plug in here.

learning_path.title: Learn the Authorization header parsing utility
learning_path.why: Every HTTP-scheme authenticator delegates raw header parsing to this single utility, and your custom scheme will need to call it to split the scheme token from the credential.
learning_path.understand: get_authorization_scheme_param partitions the Authorization header on the first space, returning (scheme, param) — call this in your __call__ to extract and validate your custom scheme prefix.

learning_path.title: Study HTTPBase's make_authenticate_headers as the challenge seam
learning_path.why: The WWW-Authenticate challenge header is assembled here and sent on 401 responses; overriding this method in your subclass is where you customize the challenge string for your scheme.
learning_path.understand: make_authenticate_headers returns the dict injected into the 401 HTTPException — override it to emit whatever challenge directive your custom scheme requires (e.g. 'MyScheme realm=…').

learning_path.title: Trace auto_error and 401 flow in HTTPBasic.__init__
learning_path.why: HTTPBasic is the simplest concrete HTTP scheme and its __init__ shows the full pattern: model registration, scheme_name defaulting to class name, realm storage, and the auto_error flag that controls whether missing credentials raise or return None.
learning_path.understand: Your custom scheme's __init__ must set self.model (an HTTPBaseModel or equivalent OpenAPI model), self.scheme_name, and self.auto_error — these three attributes are read by both the DI system and OpenAPI schema generation.

learning_path.title: Compare the OAuth2 base class __call__ and make_not_authenticated_error override
learning_path.why: OAuth2 shows the more advanced pattern: __call__ reads the Authorization header and delegates error construction to a dedicated overridable method, giving you a clean hook to customize the 401 without duplicating flow logic.
learning_path.understand: Model your custom scheme's __call__ after OAuth2.__call__ — check the header, return None or raise via a dedicated make_not_authenticated_error method — so subclasses can override the error independently of the credential-extraction logic.

learning_path.title: See how incorrect-scheme credentials produce 401 with WWW-Authenticate
learning_path.why: This test pins the exact contract your custom scheme must honour: wrong-scheme Authorization header → 401 with detail 'Not authenticated' and a correctly formatted WWW-Authenticate header matching your scheme name.
learning_path.understand: When you check credentials.scheme.lower() != 'myscheme' in __call__, you must raise HTTPException(401, headers=make_authenticate_headers()) — this test pattern is the acceptance criterion for correct scheme rejection.

learning_path.title: Wire the optional (auto_error=False) path using Security()
learning_path.why: The optional-credential pattern — Security(security) typed as T | None — is the final integration surface your users will touch, and this test shows that auto_error=False must make __call__ return None instead of raising.
learning_path.understand: Declare your dependency with Security(my_scheme) and type the parameter as MyCredentials | None; your __call__ must return None (not raise) when auto_error=False and the header is absent or mismatched, exactly as shown here.

learning_path.title: Implement your custom scheme in fastapi/security/http.py
learning_path.why: HTTPDigest is the leanest existing concrete scheme — the insertion site for a new custom HTTP scheme is immediately after this class in the same file, following the same three-step pattern: __init__, make_authenticate_headers, __call__.
learning_path.understand: Add your class after HTTPDigest: call super().__init__ (or set model/scheme_name/auto_error manually), override make_authenticate_headers with your challenge string, and implement __call__ using get_authorization_scheme_param to extract and validate credentials.

learning_path.title: Understand the SecurityBase contract every scheme must satisfy
learning_path.why: This is the single extension point: any callable that is an instance of SecurityBase gets picked up by FastAPI as an auth scheme — knowing the two required attributes is the prerequisite for everything else.
learning_path.understand: Your custom scheme must be an instance of SecurityBase and expose both `model` (a Pydantic SecurityBaseModel subclass) and `scheme_name` (str); that's the entire interface contract.

learning_path.title: See how FastAPI detects security dependencies at route registration
learning_path.why: This `isinstance(unwrapped, SecurityBase)` check is the seam that classifies a dependency as a security scheme — understanding it explains why inheriting from SecurityBase (not duck-typing) is mandatory.
learning_path.understand: FastAPI identifies security deps by unwrapping the callable and checking `isinstance(..., SecurityBase)`, so your class must literally subclass SecurityBase or this check silently fails.

learning_path.title: Trace how security deps are collected per-route
learning_path.why: This property is what `get_openapi_security_definitions` iterates over; if your dependency isn't picked up here, it disappears from both the OpenAPI spec and the dependency-solving pipeline.
learning_path.understand: `_security_dependencies` filters the full dependency tree to those where `_is_security_scheme` is True, so correct inheritance is what gates inclusion in both runtime auth and OpenAPI output.

learning_path.title: Understand how model and scheme_name feed the OpenAPI spec
learning_path.why: This function reads `scheme.model` via `jsonable_encoder` and `scheme.scheme_name` to build the securityDefinitions block — your model's shape dictates what appears in `/docs`.
learning_path.understand: Your `model` attribute is serialized with `by_alias=True, exclude_none=True` into the OpenAPI security definitions dict keyed by `scheme_name`, so the Pydantic model you assign to `self.model` must serialize to a valid OpenAPI security scheme object.

learning_path.title: Study HTTPBase as the canonical implementation template
learning_path.why: HTTPBase is the most complete reference implementation: it shows the standard `__init__` (assign model + scheme_name + auto_error), the helper error factories, and the async `__call__` signature your scheme must match.
learning_path.understand: The pattern is: build and assign `self.model` in `__init__`, implement `async def __call__(self, request: Request)` to extract and validate credentials, and raise or return None based on `self.auto_error`.

learning_path.title: Compare APIKeyBase's reusable error-handling helpers
learning_path.why: APIKeyBase introduces `make_not_authenticated_error()` and `check_api_key()` as factored helpers, demonstrating a slightly different design tradeoff you may want to replicate for your scheme's credential extraction logic.
learning_path.understand: `check_api_key()` centralizes the `auto_error` branch so `__call__` stays trivial — this is the recommended pattern for schemes where credential presence is a binary check rather than a format parse.

learning_path.title: See a complete concrete subclass: HTTPBearer's scheme-specific __call__
learning_path.why: HTTPBearer shows how to override `__call__` beyond what the base does — adding a scheme-string validation step — which is the exact pattern you'll apply when your custom scheme has format requirements.
learning_path.understand: Override `__call__` to add domain-specific validation (e.g. verify token prefix, signature, or header name) after the base extraction, falling through to `make_not_authenticated_error()` or returning None on mismatch.

learning_path.title: Confirm where route registration wires the dependency into runtime handling
learning_path.why: APIRoute's `__init__` calls `get_dependant` then `get_flat_dependant`, which is when your security dependency is discovered and stored — knowing this confirms there is no additional registration step needed.
learning_path.understand: Simply passing your SecurityBase instance to `Depends()` in an endpoint or as a route-level dependency is sufficient; `APIRoute.__init__` traverses and flattens all deps automatically at app startup.

dossier.understanding: FastAPI's security system is built on a base class `SecurityBase` that all authentication schemes inherit from. A security scheme is a callable that extracts credentials from a request and returns them (or raises an HTTPException if `auto_error=True`). The scheme must have a `model` attribute (an OpenAPI schema object) and a `scheme_name` attribute. When used as a dependency via `Depends()`, FastAPI's dependency injection system recognizes it as a security dependency, extracts its OpenAPI model, and includes it in the generated OpenAPI documentation. To add a custom authentication scheme, one inherits from `SecurityBase`, implements a `__call__` async method to extract credentials from the request, and provides an OpenAPI model that describes the scheme.

The dependency system recognizes it as a SecurityBase instance and later the OpenAPI generation extracts its model and scheme_name.

flows.name: Custom Security Scheme Recognition and OpenAPI Integration

steps.what_happens: User creates a custom class inheriting from SecurityBase with model (OpenAPI schema) and scheme_name attributes

learning_path.title: Study APIKeyBase as the canonical extension template

learning_path.title: See how HTTPBase handles header parsing and WWW-Authenticate
learning_path.why: HTTPBase shows the more complex case: separating `make_authenticate_headers()` from `make_not_authenticated_error()`, and returning a structured credentials object instead of a raw string — the pattern to follow for header-based custom schemes.
learning_path.understand: Override `make_authenticate_headers()` to control the WWW-Authenticate challenge independently of the error body, and return a typed credentials object from `__call__` so callers get structured data rather than a raw string.

learning_path.title: Understand how `_is_security_scheme` gates framework recognition
learning_path.why: This cached property is the single runtime check that separates your scheme from a plain Depends — if `isinstance(unwrapped, SecurityBase)` is False, your scheme is invisible to OpenAPI generation and scope handling.
learning_path.understand: The framework unwraps the callable (e.g. functools.partial or similar wrappers) and does an isinstance check against SecurityBase, so your class must inherit from SecurityBase directly — protocol-style duck-typing is not sufficient.

learning_path.title: Trace how `_security_scheme.model` feeds the OpenAPI spec
learning_path.why: This function reads `_security_scheme.model` and `scheme_name` off every security dependency to build the OpenAPI `securityDefinitions` — the exact attributes your class must populate correctly.
learning_path.understand: The model is JSON-encoded via `jsonable_encoder(..., by_alias=True, exclude_none=True)`, so your OpenAPI model must use the correct Pydantic aliases and avoid None on required fields, or those fields will silently drop from the spec.

learning_path.title: Understand how `Security()` differs from `Depends()` for your scheme
learning_path.why: Users of your scheme must declare it with `Security()` (not `Depends()`) to attach OAuth2 scopes and trigger the OpenAPI security requirement — using `Depends()` silently skips scope propagation.
learning_path.understand: The only functional difference between `Security` and `Depends` is that `Security` carries a `scopes` list that is threaded through to the `Dependant` and ultimately into the OpenAPI spec; custom schemes should document this requirement.

learning_path.title: See where `__call__` is actually invoked during request handling
learning_path.why: Understanding where `solve_dependencies` calls your `__call__` reveals the full execution context: what request object you receive, how caching works, and when generator-based cleanup runs — all relevant if your scheme holds resources.
learning_path.understand: Your `__call__` is invoked inside the recursive `solve_dependencies` loop with the full `Request`; if `use_cache=True` (the default), a second `Security()` declaration in the same request reuses the first result without calling `__call__` again — critical if your scheme has side effects.

learning_path.title: Identify where `scheme_name` and the Dependant are wired up at route registration
learning_path.why: This is the insertion site where `get_dependant` and `get_flat_dependant` build the dependency tree that includes your security scheme — understanding this confirms where scheme detection and OpenAPI wiring happen at startup, not at request time.
learning_path.understand: The security dependency tree is frozen at route registration time inside `APIRoute.__init__` via `get_dependant` → `get_flat_dependant`; errors in your scheme's model or `scheme_name` will surface here (or at first `/openapi.json` generation), not at request time.

dossier.understanding: FastAPI's security system is built on a class hierarchy rooted at `SecurityBase`, which defines a contract that all authentication schemes must implement: a `model` attribute (OpenAPI security definition) and a `scheme_name` attribute (for identification). Security schemes are callables that extract and validate authentication credentials from requests. The system integrates with FastAPI's dependency injection through the `Depends()` and `Security()` parameter functions, which register security schemes as dependencies. When a route is defined, the dependency analyzer recognizes `SecurityBase` instances and marks them as security dependencies. These are used to: (1) extract credential values from requests, (2) generate OpenAPI security definitions for documentation, and (3) validate OAuth2 scopes when using `Security()`. To add a custom scheme, inherit from `SecurityBase`, implement a `__call__` method to extract credentials, and define an OpenAPI model representing the scheme.
